4.note: Compare accumulated-state solutions with related prefix/suffix decompositions: path sums, circular ranges, water boundaries, and two-pass constraints. Some cards deliberately show an alternative constant-space solution.

7.note: Extend feasibility reasoning to integer square roots, citation thresholds, and water levels. The H-index card shows a sorting solution and Swim in Rising Water shows a best-first solution; both also admit binary search with a suitable feasibility check.

9.note: Meeting rooms and offline interval queries extend event-based processing. Meeting rooms accumulates deltas; minimum-interval queries combine a sorted sweep with a heap.

12.note: This practice also covers parsing and simulation: nested expressions, path normalization, zigzag output, and text justification. Choose a stack only when the task has last-in-first-out dependencies.

13.note: Compare the stack template with related monotone frontiers. Trapping Rain Water is shown with two pointers; Car Fleet compresses its frontier to one arrival time after sorting.

15.note: Tree construction, serialization, quad trees, and path DP extend the recursive-contract idea. Define the helper’s return value or the inherited path state separately for each task.

18.note: Euler trails and weighted-ratio queries are labeled extensions. Reconstruct Itinerary consumes edges and builds a route on unwinding; Evaluate Division multiplies edge ratios. Neither uses ordinary shortest unweighted path logic.

19.note: Alien Dictionary builds explicit ordering constraints. Longest Increasing Path treats increasing moves as a DAG and uses memoized DFS; topological layers are another solution.

20.note: Connected-components and valid-tree problems directly use DSU. The minimum-spanning-tree comparison shows dense Prim; Kruskal is the DSU-based alternative.

21.note: The extensions distinguish path problems from other weighted-graph tasks: stop-limited flights use bounded Bellman–Ford, point connection uses Prim’s minimum spanning tree, and equation evaluation uses ratio traversal. Their correctness arguments differ from Dijkstra’s.

22.note: Some selection problems have simpler alternatives: meeting rooms can use event deltas and Task Scheduler can use a frequency formula. Their cards show those solutions and explain the heap alternatives.

24.note: The added DP practice includes decoding, subarray states, circular choices, and stock inventory with transaction limits or cooldown. A one-dimensional input does not imply one scalar state is sufficient.

25.note: Matrix and geometry extensions are included alongside grid DP: rotation, spiral traversal, Sudoku validation, simultaneous updates, quad trees, and point geometry. These are not all DP; use each card’s own reasoning rather than forcing the right/down recurrence.

26.note: Perfect Squares and Target Sum extend resource-total DP. Burst Balloons is a contrasting interval-DP extension: its state is a range and its key choice is the last balloon, not an item capacity.

27.note: Beyond two-prefix DP, practice includes center expansion for palindromes, palindrome partitioning, regex matching, and interval DP. Distinguish subsequences, contiguous substrings, and range states before choosing a recurrence.

29.note: Prefix-related extensions include a trie-guided board search, longest common prefix, length-prefixed string encoding, and KMP substring search. KMP uses a prefix-function table, not trie nodes.

30.note: Integer-arithmetic extensions cover decimal carries, Roman numerals, digit reversal, exponentiation, and factorial factors. Bitwise identities remain useful where the representation supports them; the other cards explain their own arithmetic rules.
